kuryerpolski1754075:
From Kalisz, 5 December. At Trąbczyn, five miles from Kalisz, on the hereditary estate of the
Honourable Prusimski family, the funeral of the late Honourable Paweł Prusimski, Chamberlain of His
Royal Majesty, was held, with a large attendance of related houses, of the secular [uncertain: clergy]
and of the Cistercian Fathers of the convent of Ląd. The Reverend Głowiecki, Abbot of Ląd, had been
invited to sing the High Mass, but an unexpected frost prevented his crossing the river Warta. The
sermon was preached by the Reverend Prefect of the schools of the College of the Society of Jesus at
Kalisz. The funeral oration after the procession was given by the Honourable Antoni Prusimski, his own
nephew. In the monasteries nearby, namely at Pyzdry, Konin and Kaźmierz, at the order of Her Grace
Katarzyna Prusimska, born Rozdrażewska, his widow, exequies were held on the same day, with vigils and
many Masses, for lack of room in the parish church of Trąbczyn.

zdrowie1912z10:
# On the Nutrition of the People

[720]

We know absolutely nothing about how rural people nourish themselves, or we have very inaccurate information about it. We know, for example, that our people derive their nutrition mainly from the plant world, and here potatoes constitute their daily dish, and that the people have become accustomed to satisfy their feelings of hunger mainly with potatoes. This is where our knowledge about the nutrition of the people ends. There have been attempts to calculate the quantity of food consumed by the people, but these attempts, according to me, taken from one or even several villages of a given area, too broadly generalized the obtained figures to the entire country, for it is a fact that our people nourish themselves differently, depending on the region they inhabit, and besides, in the same region the difference in the people's nutrition is enormous, and dependent on their degree of wealth: a stable hand nourishes himself differently, differently a smallholder or landless peasant, and differently a wealthy peasant. So I think that if we want to have more accurate information about the nutrition of the people, we should consider separately territories that remain in more or less similar economic conditions, and besides, we need to divide the people into

[721]

categories according to their wealth, and the collected data will only then tell us how the people in a given area nourish themselves.

For my research on the nutrition of the people, I took the Słupca district, which stretches in a narrow strip on the border of the Grand Duchy of Poznań. Since the population of the entire borderland is in more or less similar material conditions, it seems that I will not make an error if I say that the data I obtained can be extended to the entire stretch of our country lying on the Prussian border. The question of rural people's nutrition has interested me for a long time; for over a dozen years I have been collecting data and have always had the opportunity to see how differently our people nourish themselves depending on their degree of wealth.

Due to the difference in the people's nutrition, I must divide the rural population into several groups and discuss each of them separately.

So, wealthier peasants owning more than 15 morgans [unit of land measurement]. Here breakfast consists of coffee with milk, bread and butter; dinner on non-fasting days of broth and meat, meat mainly pork, though sometimes beef, mutton or veal, sometimes chicken; on fasting days potato soup, or porridge with milk, or millet soup with butter, less often pea soup and bread; afternoon snack only in summer: bread with cottage cheese; supper: milk with potatoes, or milk soup with potatoes in summer, and in winter beet soup with potatoes; older ones still drink tea with bread and butter, but mainly only in winter. I should add that I consider only the normal way of life of the peasant, I omit family celebrations such as baptisms, weddings, funeral wakes, fairs, church festivals, etc., because here, due to the low culture of our peasant, there are excesses in eating, and even more in drinking alcohol in various forms. Let us now see to what extent such nutrition is sufficient for our peasant who works hard physically. For my calculations I take the nutrition that the peasant receives on an ordinary day, so I omit such fasting days when he nourishes himself worse. I assume that the better nutrition of festive days compensates for the worse fasting days, so one can take as a norm the nutrition of an ordinary day, neither festive nor fasting.

The organism of a hard-working person, such as our peasant, needs about 50 heat units per day per kilogram of weight.

[722]

Taking the weight of an adult person as 70 kg, it will be necessary for him to receive 3500 heat units per day with food. Let us calculate the daily nutrition of this category of peasant.

1) breakfast: on average he uses a glass of milk for coffee, 
 i.e., 200 g, which gives 133 h.u. 
 sugar 15 g 60 h.u. 
 bread 300 g 654 h.u. 
 butter 30 g 279 h.u. 
 **Total 1126 h.u.**

 

2) dinner: on average 1/2 kg of meat 1045 h.u. 
 bread 200 g 436 h.u. 
 **Total 1481 h.u.**

 

3) afternoon snack: 200 g milk 135 h.u. 
 bread 200 g 436 h.u. 
 butter 100 g 820 h.u. 
 **Total 1391 h.u.**

 

4) supper: skimmed milk 300 g 120 h.u. 
 bread 200 g 436 h.u. 
 butter 100 g 820 h.u. 
 **Total 1376 h.u.**

**Overall, the daily nutrition of this category of** 
 **peasant amounts to** **5374 h.u.**

From the above calculation we see that a rich farmer nourishes himself very well, he receives more food than his organism needs, so among wealthier farmers we do not encounter thin, emaciated individuals; on the contrary, as long as such an individual does not abuse alcohol, he usually enjoys excellent health. It is different among smallholders: here nutrition is significantly worse, not to mention the fact that other hygienic conditions are also worse among these than among wealthier farmers.

Among smallholders, breakfast consists of a piece of bread or a plate of potatoes with little butter on them, with sour skimmed milk, which gives: bread or potatoes.

bread 150 g 390 h.u. 
 milk 200 g 80 h.u. 
 **Total 470 h.u.**

[723]

dinner: potatoes 300 g 282 h.u. 
 milk 300 g 120 h.u. 
 flour 50 g 130 h.u. 
 bread 100 g 260 h.u. 
 **Total 792 h.u.**

afternoon snack: bread 200 g 520 h.u. 
 butter 50 g 410 h.u. 
 **Total 930 h.u.**

supper: skimmed milk with potatoes about 1000 heat units.

So his entire daily nutrition amounts to 3192 heat units.

From the above calculation it appears that the nutrition of the smallholder is insufficient, so no wonder that among smallholders we see mainly thin, exhausted, prematurely aged individuals. A manor farmhand nourishes himself in more or less the same way; here regarding this matter the conditions are the same as among smallholders.

However, worse than the two mentioned categories of people is how a laborer working for daily wages nourishes himself. In the border strip, these people in summer go to work mainly to Prussia, and there throughout their intensive work they nourish themselves on rice, skimmed milk and potatoes. Meat, due to the high price of this food item in Prussia, they eat once a week.

So the nutrition of such a laborer in summer amounts to no more than 2000 heat units, instead of 3500\. These losses, if nota bene he earned well in summer, he compensates for himself somewhat in winter, when he works very little or does nothing at all, and nourishes himself significantly better; but if due to various circumstances his Prussian earnings were not good, he continues to starve in winter as he starved in summer. From the above it appears that except for the few rich farmers in our country, the rest nourish themselves insufficiently.

But it is not enough that our peasant nourishes himself insufficiently; there are still other circumstances that significantly impair his nutrition. Let us look at who and how prepares his food.

A rural girl who has not the slightest idea about nutrition and cooking, when she marries, prepares food for herself and her husband, so her method of food preparation is

[724]

extremely primitive, and the food cooked by her hand is tasteless and poorly digestible. The number of dishes she serves to her household members is limited to 5-6 and these she constantly cooks, and we all know how the monotony of foods affects assimilation by the organism.

To this is added the dirt and slovenliness that we mainly see in the countryside during food preparation; kitchen utensils often poorly washed cause the foods prepared in them to burn, as a result of which they are tasteless and unhealthy. Plates and spoons are often dirty, and household members, sitting down to receive food, almost never wash their hands, with dirty hands they take bread and meat and in this way often introduce disease-causing bacteria into the organism. It is not enough that the majority of people nourish themselves insufficiently; the defectiveness in food preparation and monotony impairs assimilation, and little attention to the cleanliness of utensils and hands causes disease-causing microorganisms to enter the organism, which, being non-resistant due to insufficient nutrition and hard physical work, easily succumbs to them, which is the cause of various diseases among our people.

Now let us ask what is the reason that our people pay so little attention to their nutrition. Understanding the causes will allow us to find ways to change for improvement in this direction.

Our peasant has been accustomed for centuries to look at his body as something undeserving of attention. He takes food because without it the organism cannot exist, but it is all the same to him what and how he eats, as long as he satisfies the feeling of hunger. No one has yet taught him that for the soul to be healthy, one must care that the body also does not fall into disease, so he focuses all his attention on the soul, caring little about his earthly shell. The lack of the most elementary knowledge about nutrition is the reason why he nourishes himself poorly, and the lack of education is the reason for insufficient nutrition.

So with the development of education, the nutrition of our people must also improve. Since the development of education among the people does not depend entirely on us, we should strive to ensure that our people acquire certain knowledge about nutrition, through which they would excellently improve their nutrition. Much can be done in this direction.

[725]

If rural farmers today have facilitated acquisition of knowledge about agriculture, which they greatly benefit from, and through which their wealth increases, rural housewives should also be taught to cook, to provide the organism with a sufficient amount of food, and in such a form that it can be assimilated by the digestive tract.

So to introduce changes for the better in the nutrition of our people, we need first to try to raise their wealth, which will affect the amount of food consumed by the peasant, but alongside this we need to establish as many domestic economy schools for rural girls as possible, where in addition to other necessary knowledge about hygiene, they would acquire knowledge about cooking and nutrition, and moreover, in specially written popular brochures, the people should be constantly instructed on how and what to eat.

If the people know that nutrition is not such a trivial matter as they have thought so far, that health or disease depends on good or bad nutrition, if the peasant's wife instead of today's few dishes introduces a certain variety into this area of life, which is not difficult with good intentions, if moreover the dishes are prepared tastily and served in a form that arouses appetite, our peasant will gain enormously in health: his nutrition will improve, and on the other hand, at church festivals and fairs he will avoid today's dirty little-town shambles, where he currently treats himself to sausage and blood pudding, which are truly disgusting to look at, especially since having something to eat at home, he will sometimes avoid the mindless drinking of vodka during the consumption of blood pudding and sausage in the small town.
jutrzenka1913z8:
# How Our People Dress.

[7]

The old, characteristic costume that distinguished our peasant according to the region from which he came is disappearing; only here and there remain some remnants of it, but probably not for long. Like many other things, it will soon pass into the storehouse of antiquity, as a memory and keepsake.

In the March issue of "Zdrowie" (Health), Dr. Lidmanowski draws attention to various deficiencies of today's folk attire. It is more or less uniform in each group, and these are created by the degree of wealth. A peasant with 20 or more morgans [land measurement] dresses differently than a smallholder, differently than a laborer, differently than a manor stable hand. All of them, however, sin against hygiene - some from necessity, others from ignorance and bad habit. But even the poorer ones, especially men, wear linen shirts, most often of their own making; in this respect there is no difference between them; beyond that - shoddy fair merchandise made of poor cotton material, badly cut, badly sewn and providing little warmth. They hold their trousers at the waist with a leather belt, tightened so firmly

[8]

that it cuts into the flesh. Suspenders begin to be used by those who go to work abroad. They bring back from there, besides heavily starched collars or ones made of celluloid mass with an inseparable tie of bright color, a thick knitted shirt which they put on over the white one. This is supposed to be better protection from cold, which is completed in winter by an outer jacket with lambskin fur or a padded overcoat - ordinary German junk, bought abroad for cheap money, providing little warmth and not very comfortable. The winter covering for both the smallholder peasant, the laborer and the stable hand is a sheepskin coat. It costs some fifteen rubles and must last for several years, becoming colder each year due to the wearing away of the hair. Over such a sheepskin coat, a stable hand sent on long journeys with deliveries also puts on a burka made of thick material and girds himself with a belt.

A peasant returning from America to settle on the land and work among his own people immediately stands out from his surroundings with his entire appearance. He wears a linen shirt with a starched front, collar and cuffs fastened with studs; for warmth he puts on another knitted one over it, similar long underwear, thin socks, American boots with wide toes and low heels, a woolen jacket suit, padded overcoat, a felt hat on his head, face carefully shaved without any stubble. This is how the "American" presents himself immediately after arrival. With time these distinctions fade and disappear.

In the attire of a well-to-do peasant, one can already see greater care for comfort: in winter it protects him better from cold, in summer it does not expose him to the discomforts of heat. In this sphere too, men wear a linen shirt with collar, over it a knitted one, long underwear also knitted, clothing made of thick woolen material, on their feet socks, boots, even galoshes, on their head a felt hat. For travel, a fur coat, usually sheepskin, dark-covered. In summer a linen shirt, linen long underwear, clothing made of thin cord fabric. At home, around the farm in winter, fur lambskin trousers and such a caftan, covered with dark, cheap material.

Footwear is the plague of all. The poorer ones obviously don't know socks or stockings. Peasants wear heavy, clumsy and large boots with uppers, wrapping their feet in pieces of linen called foot wraps, to which in frosts straw is added; emigrants already use boots with narrow toes, in which the toes almost overlap each other, the foot loses its shape and becomes covered with corns. Poorer women put

[9]

laced shoes made of thick leather on their bare feet - and only when going to town to market or to church; their footwear is so terrible from a hygienic standpoint that it's fortunate they wear it rarely and only for decoration; usually very tight so that the foot appears small, with narrow toes and very high heels. At home they usually go barefoot or use clogs, i.e., a type of slipper with wooden soles, without heel counters. Wealthier women and those who have been abroad already use stockings. Women's clothing is generally even less hygienic than men's. Poorer women wear a long linen shirt fastened under the neck, over it a skirt and small jacket. In winter they sometimes put on several skirts and jackets; to church a padded jacket and a large woolen shawl. Girls going to work abroad bring back corsets from there, dress in tight dresses, use cotton stockings and hats with bright artificial flowers. Those returning from America dress with even greater refinement, use fine underwear with embroidery, fashionable hats and jackets, American footwear, comfortable with wide toes, and most importantly they wear underpants - light in summer, warm in winter.

Just like clothing, everything in the peasant's house depends on his state of wealth. A poor stable hand, laborer, even a smallholder has only one bed and one set of bedding for himself, his wife and children: a large and heavy quilt, several pillows and a sheet of coarse linen covering straw. Children up to the age of 5 and 6 usually sleep with their parents, at the foot of the bed they later get their own bedding - one for several children. The bed linen is changed at most twice a year. How such sleeping with several people in one bed and under these conditions of cleanliness affects health needs no proof.

With wealth, this too improves however. Perhaps most strongly the lack of awareness among rural women affects the children. These are constantly poorly dressed, mostly barefoot and almost naked. The wind lifts short cotton dresses and strikes the exposed little legs. This poor creature will suffer before it grows into a person hardened to cold and heat.

And how in the family of such a stable hand or laborer, even a smallholder peasant, they treat a newborn! One must admire that in such a little thing life is already so hard. It comes into the world in a cold room, they place it in bedding whose warmth does not exceed a few degrees, bathe it in water often heated above 40°, bind it with swaddling clothes so it won't "break," to such a degree that the child often cries for

[10]

whole days and nights and cannot sleep. One in six will survive in such conditions, and how many will perish!

Much has already changed in our village, and this will undoubtedly change too. Greater enlightenment will come, which will bring deeper culture to the peasant hut. It may restore some of the old customs that today, despised, had to give way to novelties, but the beautiful, colorful costume of the Polish peasant, like that of the old nobleman, will remain only a memory, a precious decoration for national celebrations.
zdrowie1914z6:
# I. How Our People Live?

[432]

Huddled to the earth, almost grown into it, stands the Polish village. You would search in vain for high houses with large windows and walls covered with red tiles, such as can be seen abroad. Our village cottages are mainly clay huts, somehow cobbled together, low, dirty and cramped. Starting from the courtyard and ending with the interior of the house, everything here mocks hygiene. And no wonder: our peasant is ignorant, and therefore poor, he cannot think about the rules of hygiene because he has never heard of them at all. His concerns are limited to somehow covering his body and securing shelter from rain and snow; he cannot think about anything more because he cannot afford it, and besides, even if he could sometimes do something to improve the health conditions of his dwelling, he doesn't do it because he doesn't know what and how to do it. How can one demand from an illiterate person that he should know what positively and what negatively affects human health? As for concepts about hygiene in general, and housing hygiene in particular, our people in their overwhelming majority have not risen much above the knowledge of a savage man. In the peasant's life everything conflicts with hygiene, but the greatest discord with the latter is constituted by his dwelling. If a cultured person, when building a dwelling for himself, pays attention in the smallest details to ensure that it protects him from diseases on one hand, and on the other, that it gives him the greatest sum of comforts and pleasures, our people when building a house think only about ensuring that it protects them from violent atmospheric changes, and also from thieves, that they can somehow prepare food in their house and spend the night; they have no other requirements from their dwelling and cannot have them.

It is true that here and there one can notice a change for the better, but these improvements are very few. Among them one could count in certain rare cases the clean maintenance of the courtyard, concern that courtyard sewage should not get into the well, planting trees around the residential house, and finally, when building a house, the thought of protecting its walls from moisture. This is almost everything that our peasant has done in recent times to improve the health conditions of his dwelling, though even this is seen, as I said above, very rarely.

[433]

Over the course of many years, visiting almost daily the dwellings of our people, I had the opportunity to closely observe how these people live. In many cases I tried to become thoroughly acquainted with the dwelling of a sick person, I measured the width and length of rooms in steps, and the height I often estimated by eye, sometimes measured. It is understood that such measurements cannot claim precision, but they prove themselves sometimes; I came to the conviction that the height of rooms, estimated by eye, differed from the actual only in a few cases, while the length of my steps was 3/5 of a meter. In this way I examined 1200 dwellings of independent farmers, i.e., people who have their own cottage and their own farm; I examined 80 dwellings of stable hands and manor laborers, and 140 dwellings of people who either work for daily wages in the country or go out for summer work abroad.

Before I proceed to describe the dwellings themselves, I want to devote a few words to the surroundings of the residential house and describe the material from which the houses of our peasants are built. So the first and last category of peasants, i.e., independent farmers as well as seasonal laborers, since the latter often live with the former, have mainly quadrangular courtyards, usually located by the road running through the village; the residential house stands at the front, opposite the house is the barn, and on the sides are cowsheds, stables and pigsties. The house usually does not stand right by the road, but somewhat removed from the road, and in front of the house is a small garden with a few fruit trees, where in summer, to beautify the house, the farmer diligently sows some flowers. In the courtyard, not far from the cowsheds and stables, is the manure pile. In the middle of the courtyard, often very close to the manure pile, is the well. A latrine in the peasant's courtyard is something almost completely unknown.

The houses of manor people also mostly stand by the road, but the courtyards at these houses, to save land, are so small that the pigsties standing opposite the houses are separated from the houses by only a few cubits of space.

The material from which our peasants' houses are built is mainly clay; old houses from former times are wooden; currently they build from wood very rarely due to the price of this material; sometimes they build from iron ore in localities where ore is found. Hewn cubes of ore are joined together with clay. In recent times they build more often with brick; since they use mainly clay for joining bricks, the wealthier ones lay the foundation and about a cubit above the foundation with lime, higher they used only clay. The covering

[434]

of houses is mainly straw, which they use because of the cheapness of this material and its durability, and also because straw covering protects more in summer from heat and in winter from cold, though from the standpoint of fire safety it is the worst material one can imagine. Houses built of clay are usually plastered and whitewashed; those of ore and brick are left unplastered.

Of the 1200 dwellings of rural farmers, 13 consisted of a kitchen and two rooms, 86 of a kitchen and a room, the rest, i.e., 1101, consisted of one room that serves as kitchen, living room and bedroom; that is, in percentages, discarding fractions, the dwellings of rural people are represented as: 2 rooms and kitchen 1%, one room and kitchen 7%, the rest 91% is one single room. Dwellings consisting of two rooms and a kitchen belong to wealthy farmers; such a dwelling always occupies a separate house, divided by a hallway into two halves. The hallway in the middle of the house goes through the entire width of it and is divided by a wall into two halves; the front one with front doors, from this hallway on one side leads the entrance to one room, from the other to the other. The hallway is entered only from the courtyard; from it one side leads to the kitchen, the other to a storeroom. In the room adjacent to the kitchen there is something like a dining room; in the middle stands a table and several chairs, around the walls are beds for children. The room on the other side of the house is the bedroom of the household; in it stand 2 beds, a table, a wardrobe and chairs. The beds are high, made up with bedding, on the walls are holy pictures. This room serves as a bedroom for the household only in the summer season, but in winter everything gathers in the kitchen and the room adjacent to it. During frosts, everyone even leaves this room and fits into the kitchen, because it is warmer there. The whole year the life of the rich peasant centers on the kitchen; here the whole family constantly stays in moments free from farm work, here they eat, here they deliberate over their affairs, only for rest do they go to the room. The household's bedroom, rarely visited by household members, which children are almost completely forbidden to enter, is usually kept in exemplary order, but the room adjacent to the kitchen, being more frequently visited, no longer sins with cleanliness: the floor is usually dirty and all the furnishings leave much to be desired in terms of cleanliness. Here stand several beds intended for children and for the household's daily use. Of 13 dwellings of this type, in 8 I found tile stoves, in 3 a tile stove in the household's room, an iron one in the children's room, in two iron stoves

[435]

in the room adjacent to the kitchen; in the household's room there was no stove at all. The plan of the wealthy peasant's house, just described, is so beloved by the wealthy farmer that I know of cases where a peasant, buying a house still quite good but in a different plan than this one, preferred to completely demolish it and build a house according to the plan beloved by himself.

Windows in the house, two in each room and kitchen, usually single, though sometimes double ones already occur. The windows are on hinges, they open well, but the owner of the dwelling rarely takes advantage of this in summer, and never in winter.

The kitchen is usually smaller than the rooms; in one corner it has a masonry stove for cooking, the so-called kettle, with two plates for 4 pots. Stoves for baking bread are usually in the hallway. Since in a larger household one cooks constantly either for household members or for livestock and cattle, the fire therefore does not go out in the kitchen stove for whole days, so in the kitchen it is always hot, and the air is saturated with steam and emanations from cooking potatoes, turnips and cabbage. So that the kitchen stove would better heat the kitchen in winter, they arrange it so that smoke from the kitchen stove is not released directly to the chimney, but is conducted through tin pipes several cubits long, which, heating up from the smoke circulating through them, heat the air of the kitchen. In summer these pipes are either removed, or by means of special devices - dampers - smoke is directly admitted to the chimney.

The kitchen is the place where the entire life of the farm owner, his family and servants centers, so especially in winter, when the doors to the hallway are closed, the air in the kitchen is unbearable. Of 13 such houses, the kitchen on average had 24 cubic meters, and since the number of inhabitants in these houses together with servants was 109 people, so on average 8 people per dwelling crowd together, especially in the winter season, in the kitchen.

The dwelling just described is the best that can be seen among rural people. Although the kitchen is too small, although in terms of cleanliness it sometimes leaves much to be desired, though it is cramped, it is still much better than the dwellings of poorer peasants. Here at least the household and family have other quarters for the night, where there is more air and where relative cleanliness prevails.

[436]

But how few such dwellings there are! Barely 1% of all rural dwellings.

I now proceed to describe dwellings of the second category, i.e., consisting of a room and kitchen.

At the outset we must note that regarding the cleanliness of these dwellings, one can observe colossal differences. In some we see order and cleanliness, in others dirt and slovenliness pushed to impossible limits. The cause of this is the housewife. Where she is a more intelligent and industrious woman, there it is quite clean and one can see order and arrangement; where the woman is dull and lazy, there can be no talk of order and cleanliness.

In dwellings of this category we mainly see wooden floors in the room and kitchen; only in 42 out of 86 there was no floor in both rooms, and of these 42, in 23 there was no floor either in the room or in the kitchen. Windows small, mainly without hinges, and therefore unable to open; stoves in the room molded from clay, rarely tiled, often made of sheet metal; in the kitchen a clay stove with a huge opening, in which pots during cooking stand on iron supports, or are hung on wires attached to the vault of the stove. Currently one more often sees attached to such a chimney a stove of cast iron with openings and fireboxes. In certain households they arrange it so that the chimney, as a place for cooking, is used only in summer, and in winter the iron stove. This is done so that during summer heat the kitchen temperature is not raised too much, and in winter the iron stove is used so that while cooking, the kitchen is also heated.

The construction of houses is faulty, mainly molded from clay. Of 86 dwellings, 14 were built of brick, a cubit above ground level with lime, higher with clay; the rest, 72, molded from clay. In all, moisture can be observed to a lesser or greater degree.

Many of this category of dwellings are dwellings in newly built houses, mainly on plots of land recently acquired. The inhabitants of these houses are former foreign workers who, having saved up some money through their hard work, bought land and built cottages on it. Since they spent almost all their savings on buying land, not much remained for building the house, so of necessity they must build as cheaply as possible. So they mold cottages from clay, which they have on their ground, cover with straw, which their own land gives them; in the dwelling they give no floor at all, or

[437]

somehow beat one out of clay. With time, when their material situation improves, this immediately affects their dwelling, though they then do more to beautify their dwelling according to their taste than for hygiene. Sometimes, however, something is also done to improve the health conditions of the dwelling.

The owners of one-room dwellings are the poorest agricultural farmers, people who have barely a few morgans of land each. The cottage of such a peasant is a miserable clay hut, part of which is intended for living, part for storing potatoes, cabbage, a small amount of grain and various junk. In almost half of such dwellings, namely 480, there was no floor at all; bare earth or a thin layer of clay constituted the floor. The dimensions of these rooms do not exceed 8x6 meters of floor area, while the smallest cottage had 2 meters width and 5 length. Stoves in these rooms are only sheet metal. Windows mainly tiny, never opening. There is still one peculiarity of these rooms, which is not found in the dwellings described above, namely in rooms where there is a floor laid from boards, there is usually an entrance to a cellar, called a basement; since in these basements there is storage of potatoes, beets and other root vegetables, vapors therefore get through poorly fitted boards into the room and poison its air.

If the dwellings of rural farmers, especially the poorer ones, leave much to be desired from a hygienic standpoint, if there we encounter moisture almost everywhere, and very often cramped conditions and dirt, if the comfort of these dwellings stands below the minimal requirements of a cultured person, then the dwellings of manor servants present themselves quite desperately. Of 80 quarters of this type that I examined, I did not find a single one that was somehow good, although we encounter certain differences in the manor worker's dwelling depending on how much the estate owner cares for his people; however, I did not see a single dwelling about which one could say that from a hygienic standpoint it is completely good. In general one can say that these people live worst of all peasants. All 80 dwellings that I saw were one small room; in only 3 I saw a wooden floor, the rest have clay floors. All dwellings are damp, some more, others less; I did not find a single dwelling without moisture, but I also saw such moisture that the walls were literally wet all over. Since sleeping by such a damp wall is very unpleasant, these people therefore manage in such a way that

[438]

either they place beds not right against the wall, but somewhat away from it, or more often, they pin straw mats against such a damp wall or attach straw to the wall by means of boards, and in this way protect themselves at least partially from very unpleasant and unhealthy moisture. The rooms are mainly small: the floor area of the largest room was 6x4 meters, the smallest 3x2 meters. Stoves everywhere are iron kitchens, which heat the room only when one cooks on them; however, the moment the fire goes out, the room temperature drops sharply. Window mainly one, only in 16 were there 2 windows; they rarely have devices for opening for ventilation of the room, almost everywhere they are nailed shut. The small windows illuminate the room too scantily, and flowers placed on the windows let even less light into the dwelling. Beside the room, in 8 dwellings, I found a pantry for storing cabbage, potatoes, etc.; in the rest of the dwellings this was completely absent, so people living in such rooms have barrels of cabbage next to the bed, and under the bed storage of potatoes. In one dwelling I found a cowshed adjacent to the room, in which besides a cow with calf, pigs also nested; the entrance from that room to the cowshed was directly from the room. One can imagine what kind of air there could be in the room!

Whitewashing the walls of the room is done once a year, usually before Easter holidays, when generally a thorough cleaning is done in the room. Throughout the year under beds, wardrobes and other furniture, garbage is not swept out at all.

The walls above the beds are abundantly decorated with various holy pictures bought at fairs; sometimes 20 pieces hang there, and everything is abundantly covered with dust and dirt, and behind them vermin nests.

The entire furnishing of a manor farmhand's room consists of one or more beds according to the number of family members, a cradle, a low cupboard with shelves for placing pots of milk, on such a cupboard there are usually shelves on which they place plates, glasses and hang spoons, a table, one, two, at most three chairs, a large chest serving for storing linen and a barrel of cabbage. This is the entire wealth of a manor hired hand.

If the life of this category of peasants presents itself worse in every respect than others, then in terms of dwelling their conditions are deplorable. In winter cold, in summer unbearable heat, moisture, dirt and misery - this is the lot of these people; no wonder then that

[439]

stronger people, not burdened with small children, abandon such thankless service and in summer go to work abroad, as this gives them the possibility of better maintenance than in manor service. Only the weaker or those burdened with several small children are forced to agree to the miserable conditions of life in general, and dwelling in particular, and only these now remain in service at the manor.

Although a stable hand, abandoning manor service and going to work abroad, does not much improve the conditions of his dwelling, nevertheless in general it must be admitted that he lives more tolerably than in the times of manor service. Seasonal agricultural workers going abroad mainly rent dwellings for themselves in the city and here spend the winter months. All 140 dwellings that I examined were one-room dwellings. These people have neither cattle nor livestock; in their dwellings no food is cooked and prepared for animals, as a result of which in these dwellings the air is not saturated with vapors from cooking beets, potatoes, cabbage; next, in the dwelling of a seasonal worker there is usually more cleanliness than at a manor worker's, probably for the same reason, and also because during his stay abroad he became more accustomed to maintaining cleanliness in his dwelling, and mainly probably because having free time, he can care more for cleanliness and order in his dwelling. Although dwellings of this category of people are rarely dry - of 140 dwellings I found barely 32 dry - although these dwellings too are cramped: the largest room had a floor area of 5x6 m, the smallest 3x4 m, nevertheless in all I found wooden floors and windows that could open. In general, a seasonal worker, when renting a dwelling, makes certain demands on the house owner, which the latter must satisfy, while a manor servant regarding dwelling must take what they give him and have no requirements in this regard. However, although a seasonal worker generally lives better than a manor worker, this does not mean that his dwelling is good; on the contrary, there are great deficiencies here that he must accept. Among the deficiencies of these dwellings belongs the faulty arrangement of the stove, mainly an iron kitchen stove; next, these dwellings are too cramped, but a seasonal worker cannot afford more spacious ones, as he cannot afford it; the money earned during summer must be calculated so that it lasts him through winter until spring, when he will again set out abroad far away to earn himself some money for his further miserable existence.

[440]

Summarizing everything I have said, one can draw the following conclusion: the dwellings of rural people are bad in many respects, and mainly from a hygienic standpoint. Rooms mainly cramped, not ventilated at all, with faulty construction of stoves, dirty and dark, do not contribute at all to the health of our peasant; moreover, uncovered wells with primitive methods of drawing water must often constitute a cause of diseases among our people. In short, it is bad. What is the cause of this? Without doubt the most important cause is the ignorance of our people. It is difficult to demand from an ignorant person that he should arrange a hygienic dwelling for himself when he has no idea what badly and what well affects his health. A ray of light, sent under the peasant's thatch, will make colossal changes in his material situation, and thereby also in the conditions of his dwelling. This can already be seen among more enlightened farmers, who instead of using money on worthless things in the dwelling, care more about improving the dwelling from a hygienic standpoint, either by putting up better stoves than they had before, or by building houses with more spacious dwellings and better windows, or they care about the cleanliness of water in the well, knowing that contamination of well water can be a cause of disease.

In today's conditions, however, our peasant is constrained in many respects. Though he sometimes already knows how one should build, he must build not as he should build and as he would like, but as he can, though he knows he is doing wrong. He is forced, for example, sometimes to build a clay hut, though he knows that such a house is almost always damp, and he does this because brick in his conditions is too expensive a material, and it is expensive for the reason that those who engage in brick manufacturing impose such a high price on it that the peasant's pocket cannot afford it; the same applies to other building materials.

Middlemen engaged in selling these things draw large profits, while our peasant has no possibility of acquiring for himself what would amply pay him back in terms of health and other respects. Moreover, the lack of cheap and long-term credit completes the rest. No wonder then that with so many unfavorable circumstances our peasant lives as he lives. Education and the development of sound cooperatives can do much here and surely will, and then our people will undoubtedly live differently than they live today.
echotureckie1931018:
A disturbance in Zagórów.

On 24 April of this year the little town of Zagórów in the Słupca district was
the scene of violent clashes, in connection with the recruiting of seasonal
workers for work in Germany.

For some days now a so-called recruiting commission has been sitting in the
town, taking on workers for the seasonal work in Germany.

Yesterday a huge crowd of workers gathered in front of the commission's
premises, demanding to be taken on for the seasonal work.

As the quota was already exhausted, the commission's chairman declared that he
could take on no more people.

Thereupon the crowd took on a threatening air and began to bombard the
premises with stones.

Notified of the disturbances, the starosta of the powiat at Słupca came to
Zagórów with considerable reinforcements of police, which moved in to
intervene.

At the sight of the navy-blue uniforms the workers again stormed the premises,
showering the police and the members of the commission with a hail of stones.

The police drawn up in front of the premises set about dispersing the crowd.
Only in the afternoon hours did calm return. The police arrested a dozen or
more persons

who had incited the crowd.
kurjerpoznanski19330712:
Hitlerized colonists

The neighbourhood of Zagórów — that is, the rural communes of Oleśnica,
Trąbczyn and Szymanowice — is inhabited by a fair number of German
colonists. The colonies they live in once bore German names, e.g.
Emilienhain, Ludwigslust and so on. Since Hitler took power in Germany,
something, it would seem, has turned over in this population's heads. For
example, when conducting business at the commune office they make
themselves heard not in Polish but in German. Then again, the children of
these colonists who attend school answer in German when they are greeted
with the words "dzień dobry" (good day). Recently an incident occurred: on
the arrival of the school inspector at one of the schools, where an
Evangelical taught, not one of the German colonists' children came to
school. The teacher of that school was dismissed from his post after the
incident.
dziennikpoznanski19370807:
From Zagórów

Recruitment of the unemployed for Germany

During the last recruitment of seasonal agricultural workers for Germany,
about sixty people were sent off from the town of Zagórów, more than one of
whom has already sent his family a little of his hard-earned cash. Through
the workers' departure the municipal budget has been relieved, (mat)

The moving of the old people's home

The old people's home, so far housed in a building rented from Mrs Wiznerowa
in Zagórów, as its rooms did not answer, has been moved by the Municipal
Board to a property belonging to the heirs of Ignacy Ciszewski, in the
village and commune of Oleśnica, some 300 metres from the home as it has
stood. The property, now let, is in a brick building by the highway leading
from Zagórów through Oleśnica to Konin, in which, besides the home, nobody
else will live, and the old folk will have the fresh air and the full freedom
of the adjoining garden, which will in addition tell well on their aged
years. The supervision of the home has been entrusted to the deputy mayor of
the Municipal Board at Zagórów, Mr Franciszek Łukaszewski, (mat)

From the town's management

The Board of the town of Zagórów, wishing the town to have a comely
appearance, has set about building pavements; the work has been begun, and
along these pavements trees will be planted, adorning the town, (mat)
ostdeutscherbeobachter19420197:
# 225-Year-Old German Settlement in the Wartheland

# **Silesians founded the present Lazinsk cantor's school in 1718 until 1933**

The attentive observer will repeatedly come across things that testify to the work and life of our ancestors in the East.

In the most diverse areas of our large Gau (district), proof of the preceding thesis can be provided in the clearest possible way.

In remote communities or villages, we often unexpectedly encounter a piece of German history, hearing and reading about hard, fateful struggles that German people had to endure among foreign ethnicities long ago.

If one leaves the district town of Konin along the Warta River in a southwesterly direction, they soon reach the administrative district of Drommin, which, alongside Michalinow, includes the purely German settlement of Lazinsk. We were fortunate and met the ethnic German teacher and farmer Mielke, with whom we had a long conversation and who had so much interesting information to share that truly deserves to be recorded.

The year was 1718 when 14 German families from Silesia, led by the village headman, set out as pioneers of German cultural will, heading east to seek a new home, which they eventually found in what is now the community of Lazinsk. Some of these families can be proven to have borne the names Kuhn, Merk, Schönfisch, and Haupt. These are names that can still be found in Lazinsk today, a village that now consists of approximately 170 families.

[Picture]
*A view of the ancient cantor school in Lazinsk - Photo: Spatz*

To the left of the old cantor school, which we will discuss later, lies a small, unusually tree-filled cemetery on a gently rising hill, which was established by our ancestors with the first grave in 1727. At this ancient burial site, marked by weathered and decayed grave markers, signs of decay remind us of a time long past. Here, we still find the tradition of wooden or iron grave tablets, a custom long forgotten in the large German Reich. While the old Reich territory kept pace with the development of modern technology, which also introduced new methods in cemetery maintenance, the Germans, surrounded by foreign ethnic groups, held onto this old tradition.

The cantor school, where church services were also held, is also of considerable age. Its modest and simple construction stands as a grey witness from a long-gone era, speaking to us of the work of German people. Until 1933, German children were still being taught in the old cantor school! It was in that year that teacher Mielke made the noble and significant decision for the German people to build a new German school, at his own expense, not far from the old cantor school. It is important to note that this happened in 1933, the year when Adolf Hitler took control of the Reich's destiny. The historical events likely acted as a beacon for this ethnic German fighter when he made this bold decision. However, the Poles only allowed him to continue for four more years before they believed they also had to neutralise this German. They simply transferred him to Galicia and unlawfully appropriated the school, immediately declaring it a Polish school. In 1939, they dismissed the deserving teacher altogether because, even in his Galician exile, he seemed too "dangerous" to them.

But as so often happens, fate moved swiftly, delivering judgement on a people who had taken on an indelible blood guilt by their cruel struggle against innocent Germans. When the Polish state collapsed in 18 days under the weight of German blows in the early autumn of 1939, bringing long-awaited freedom to the German people in the Wartheland, the expelled farmer and teacher returned to his village of Lazinsk without hesitation. He resumed teaching in the now once again German school, where he has been the director since 1940.

Currently, four teachers care for 153 German children. In addition to the teacher, his sister and two young teachers from Thuringia work at the school. They all unanimously stated how much joy the schoolwork in the community of Lazinsk brings them, a place that had so much history to tell.

Thus, we took our leave of this settlement, which 14 German families from Silesia founded in 1718. The settlement has preserved its German identity through the continuous struggle against Slavdom, and its steadfast perseverance found its greatest reward in the return to the great German fatherland.

*Willi Spatz.*
luteraniezagorow:
Zagórów, the filial of the Evangelical-Augsburg Parish in Konin

The more important events in the life of the Parish in Zagórów

In the sixteenth century the Reformation movement was conducted by the monks of Ląd.

[Picture]

In the years 1720 - 1817 evangelicals arrived from Silesia, Pomerania and Prussia. They founded villages, raised chapels, and were given pastoral care by the incumbent of the evangelical parish at Września.

In the years 1817 - 1856 the care was exercised by the incumbents of the parishes
of Grodziec, Konin and Żychlin.
In Zagórów a filial of the parish of Grodziec was founded.

[Picture]

1856 - on 24 December the erecting of the Parish
in Zagórów.

1857 - the Parish bought the plot for the building of the Church.

1878 - on 8 May the laying of the foundation stone for the Church.

1882 - on the first Sunday in Advent, the consecration of the Church.

1913 - the building of the cantor's house.

1938 - on 16 October the consecration of the rectory.

1954 - on 18 July the first service after the Second World War. It was celebrated by the Rev. Karol Świtalski.

1995 - on 16 June the consecration of the former cantor's house as the Evangelical Senior Citizens' Home, performed by
His Excellency the Rev. Bishop Michał Warczyński.

2008 - on 17 August a new electronic clock and electronic bells.

2009 - on 30 November the Evangelical Senior Citizens' Home ended its activity (read more).
twojaslupca20150706:
Trąbczyn celebrated 775 years

6 July 2015

[Picture]

Trąbczyn is 775 years old this year. The jubilee was celebrated yesterday.
There was a little history, thanks and honours, and plenty of good fun.

The history of Trąbczyn is very rich. The place of Trąbczyn — or rather
Trampczin — is named for the first time in a medieval document of the year
1240. It concerns the grant by the Archbishop of Gniezno of tithes from
several villages, Trąbczyn among them, to the Cistercian monastery at Ląd.
The first documented owner of the village, from the grant of Duke Bolesław
the Pious, was Janek, son of Szymon. After him come the further heirs: the
count of Ląd, Mikołaj, the count Jan, and Przedpełk. To the end of the
seventeenth century the estates of Trąbczyn were in the hands of the
Trąbczyński family of the coat of arms Dryja. Later the owners changed
several times more. Many of the heirs of Trąbczyn and their descendants took
an active part in the wars of national liberation. Among them were, among
others, Antoni Prusimski, Stanisław Count Miączyński, and Aleksander and
Włodzimierz Miączyński. To honour their memory and to bring the history of
the little homeland near to the young generation, the celebrations of the
775th anniversary of the village's foundation were held yesterday in
Trąbczyn.

The celebrations were opened by a Mass in the parish church of St Stanislaus,
Bishop and Martyr. After it the memorial tablet and the obelisk were
unveiled. The further part of the jubilee took place on the ground by the
School-and-Gymnasium Complex named for the European Union in Trąbczyn. To
begin, all the guests were welcomed and the honours "Zasłużony dla wsi
Trąbczyn" — "Meritorious for the village of Trąbczyn" — were presented. They
were received by: Wiesław Radniecki Andrzej Kin [the print runs the two names
together], Marcin Urycki, Jan Nowak, Andrzej Przygoński, Robert Kaczmarek,
Stanisław Grajewski, Maria Urbaniak, Elżbieta Bączkiewicz, Ryszard Duda,
Paweł Kin, Irena Kubacka, Sławomir Swędrowski, Joanna Kicińska, Gabriel
Kubiak, Renata Kałużna, Kamila Witkiewicz, Marzena kazimierska [as printed],
Alicja Szymkowiak, Lech Wojciechowski, Krystyna Wojciechowska, Maciej
Urbaniak, Tadeusz Osowiec, Irena Zielińska, Tadeusz Krotoszyński, Juliusz
Fagasiński, Grzegorz Kucharczyk, Roman Kaczmarek, Stanisława Musielska,
Jadwiga Bartczak, Wanda Matecka, Maria Antkowiak, Zofia Wojtyra, Ryszard
Musiałowski, Anna Siuba, Marianna Nowaczyk, Marianna Graczyk, Krystyna
Kozioł, Stanisław Przydryga, Artur Paprzycki, Andrzej Drop, Adrian
Krajewski, Janusz Lewicz, Jadwiga Grajewska, Leon Parus, Anna Siuba [named
above], Józef Wolicki and Józef Kozioł. Posthumously the title "Zasłużony
dla wsi Trąbczyn" was also conferred on Krystyna Reszkiewicz. All the
invited guests were also given commemorative statuettes.

On the occasion of the jubilee the exhibition "775 lat Trąbczyna" —
"775 years of Trąbczyn" — describing the history of the village was also
officially opened. Local young people presented themselves on the stage;
many interesting games and competitions were prepared for the children; and
the star of the evening was the band Skaner. The day closed with a dance.
